understand.title: Understanding blood donation
understand.lead: What a donation is used for, the journey of a blood bag from drive to patient, and a few key figures.
understand.metaDescription: What a blood donation is used for, the journey of a blood bag from drive to patient, and the key figures, explained simply.

purpose.title: What a donation is used for
purpose.intro: Blood cannot be manufactured. Every bag collected is separated into several products that meet very different needs.

transfusion.title: Emergencies and surgery
transfusion.body: Bleeding after an accident or childbirth, major surgery, severe burns: transfusion makes up for rapid blood loss.

chronic.title: Blood diseases and cancers
chronic.body: Sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, leukaemia and other cancers require regular transfusions, sometimes for life.

plasma.title: Plasma-derived medicines
plasma.body: Plasma is used to make treatments for immune disorders, haemophilia and some rare diseases.

journey.title: The journey of a blood bag
journey.intro: Between your arm and a patient's, every bag follows a process that is checked at each step.

s1.title: Collection
s1.body: 8 to 10 minutes for a whole blood donation, roughly 420 to 480 mL depending on your weight.

s2.title: Biological screening
s2.body: Every donation is tested (blood group, screening for transmissible infections) before any use.

s3.title: Preparation
s3.body: The bag is separated into red cells, plasma and sometimes platelets, to treat several patients.

s4.title: Distribution
s4.body: Products are delivered to hospitals according to their needs and current stock levels.

s5.title: Transfusion
s5.body: The product is given to the patient after a final compatibility check at the bedside.

whoItHelps.title: Who it helps
whoItHelps.lead: Donation mostly helps people you never see: patients with chronic conditions for whom transfusion is part of life.
whoItHelps.metaDescription: Sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, Steinert's disease: three conditions where blood donation changes patients' daily lives.
whoItHelps.personaDisclaimer: The quotes below reflect real situations but are personas, not identifiable people.

sickleCell.name: Sickle cell disease
sickleCell.what: A genetic disorder of the red blood cell, the most common in France. Cells become misshapen, block vessels and cause intense pain crises.
sickleCell.howBloodHelps: Regular transfusions, sometimes full blood exchanges, dilute the affected cells and prevent serious complications such as stroke.
sickleCell.quote: Without my transfusions every four weeks, I could not work or look after my children.

cysticFibrosis.name: Cystic fibrosis
cysticFibrosis.what: A genetic disease that clogs the lungs and digestive system. Life expectancy has improved a lot, but the disease remains heavy.
cysticFibrosis.howBloodHelps: Lung transplants and digestive surgery, common in advanced forms, use large amounts of blood products.
cysticFibrosis.quote: My transplant lasted eight hours. Several donors were needed just for me that day.

steinert.name: Steinert's disease
steinert.what: The most common form of myotonic dystrophy in adults: progressive muscle weakness, heart and multi-organ involvement.
steinert.howBloodHelps: Patients undergo repeated procedures (heart, cataract, general surgery) where transfusion makes the operation safer.
steinert.quote: With every operation, the question of available blood comes up. We think about it for our relatives too — the disease is hereditary.

eligibility.title: Can I donate?
eligibility.lead: A questionnaire based on the official EFS criteria. The result is indicative: the pre-donation interview prevails.

about.title: About
about.lead: Bon Sang is a personal, independent project. Here are its sources, its method and what it does with your data.
about.metaDescription: Bon Sang: an independent site about blood donation. Sources, methodology, privacy and legal notices.

independence.title: An independent site
independence.body: Bon Sang is not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by the Établissement français du sang. For anything official (appointments, donating), use the EFS website.

sources.title: Sources
sources.body: Medical information and eligibility criteria come from the EFS public documentation. The blood drives shown come from its open data.
sources.associations: Patient associations mentioned: SOS Globi, Vaincre la Mucoviscidose, AFM-Téléthon.

method.title: Eligibility test methodology
method.body: The "Can I donate?" questionnaire follows the main criteria published by the EFS. Its result is indicative: only the medical interview before donating can confirm that you can donate.

privacy.title: Your data
privacy.body: No account, no server. Your donation log, your reminders and the test result stay in your browser and are sent nowhere. No advertising trackers.

tech.title: How it is built
tech.body: A static site built with Next.js and TypeScript, bilingual French / English. The code is open source.
